x.KJV: She maketh fine linen, and selleth it; and delivereth girdles unto the merchant.
x.YLT: Linen garments she hath made, and selleth, And a girdle she hath given to the merchant.

nt: Here, **a linen garment**, **a belt**, and **the Canaanite** refer to these things and people in general. If it would be helpful, you could use more natural expressions in your language. Alternate translation: [linen garments … belts … to Canaanites]

Lemuel’s mother is leaving out a word that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You could supply this word from the context if it would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and sells that garment]

Here, **gives** means that she supplies this **belt** to a **Canaanite** who is a merchant and so pays her for the item and then sells it to others. It does not refer to giving the **belt** away for free. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [she supplies]

Here, **Canaanite** refers specifically to **Canaanite** traders. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to the Canaanite trader] or [to someone who trades goods]

x.ASV: Strength and dignity are her clothing; And she laugheth at the time to come.
x.Darby: Strength and dignity are her clothing, and she laugheth [at] the coming day.
x.KJV: Strength and honour are her clothing; and she shall rejoice in time to come.
x.YLT: Strength and honour are her clothing, And she rejoiceth at a latter day.

nt: Here Lemuel’s mother speaks of this woman having **Strength and splendor** that other people notice. It’s as if she were wearing those qualities as **clothing** that other people could see. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly or use a simile. Alternate translation: [Everyone notices her strength and splendor] or [People notice her strength and splendor as if they were her clothing]
See how you translated the abstract nouns **Strength** in [5:10](../05/10.md) and **splendor** in [4:9](../04/09.md).

Here, the woman **laughs** because she feels confident and cheerful about what will happen in the future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and she is confident about a future day]

Here, **a future day** refers to what will happen in the future. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [at what will happen in the future]

x.ASV: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; And the law of kindness is on her tongue.
x.Darby: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and upon her tongue is the law of kindness.
x.KJV: She openeth her mouth with wisdom; and in her tongue is the law of kindness.
x.YLT: Her mouth she hath opened in wisdom, And the law of kindness is on her tongue.

nt: Here, **mouth opens** refers to speaking. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [She talks]
See how you translated the abstract noun **wisdom** in [1:2](../01/02.md).

Here, Lemuel’s mother is using the possessive form to describe **the law** that is characterized by **covenant faithfulness**. If your language would not use the possessive form for this, you could use a different expression. Alternate translation: [and the law that is characterized by covenant faithfulness]

Although **the law** here is singular, it refers to what this woman teaches or instructs others. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and the instructions of] or [and the teachings of]
See how you translated the same use of **covenant faithfulness** in [11:17](../11/17.md).

Here, **on her tongue** refers to her speaking, which involved using **her tongue**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [is spoken by her]

x.ASV: She looketh well to the ways of her household, And eateth not the bread of idleness.
x.Darby: She surveyeth the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.
x.KJV: She looketh well to the ways of her household, and eateth not the bread of idleness.
x.YLT: She is watching the ways of her household, And bread of sloth she eateth not.

nt: Here, **the goings on of her house** could refer to: (1) what happens inside her home. Alternate translation: [what happens in her home]; (2) what the people who live in **her house** do, in which case **her house** has the same meaning as in [31:15](../31/15.md). Alternate translation: [what her family does]

Here, Lemuel’s mother speaks of someone being lazy as if **laziness** were **bread** that a person **eats**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and she does not act idly]

x.ASV: Her children rise up, and call her blessed; Her husband also, and he praiseth her, saying:
x.Darby: Her children rise up and call her blessed; her husband [also], and he praiseth her:
x.KJV: Her children arise up, and call her blessed; her husband also, and he praiseth her.
x.YLT: Her sons have risen up, and pronounce her happy, Her husband, and he praiseth her,

nt: See how you translated the same use of **sons** in [4:1](../04/01.md).

Here, the phrase **rise up** refers to a symbolic action to show respect for someone. If this would not be clear to your readers, you could explain the significance of this action in the text or in a footnote. Alternate translation: [stand to show respect]

x.ASV: Many daughters have done worthily, But thou excellest them all.
x.Darby: Many daughters have done worthily, but thou excellest them all.
x.KJV: Many daughters have done virtuously, but thou excellest them all.
x.YLT: `Many are the daughters who have done worthily, Thou hast gone up above them all.'

nt: רַבּ֣וֹת בָּ֭נוֹת עָ֣שׂוּ חָ֑יִל וְ֝⁠אַ֗תְּ עָלִ֥ית עַל־כֻּלָּֽ⁠נָה

This verse is a quotation of what the woman’s husband said. If it would be helpful in your language, you could indicate this with quotation marks or with whatever other punctuation or convention your language uses to indicate a quotation.
Here, the woman’s husband uses **daughters** to refer to women in general. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly, as in the UST.
Here, **worth** refers to both physical ability and moral **worth**. See how you translated the same use of **worth** in [31:10](../31/10.md).

The woman’s husband uses the word **yourself** to emphasize how excellent his wife is. Use a way that is natural in your language to indicate this emphasis. Alternate translation: [but you, yes, you have ascended]

Here, the woman’s husband speaks of his wife acting more admirably than all other woman as if she **ascended over** them. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [but you yourself have acted more worthily than] or [but you yourself are more excellent than]

x.ASV: Grace is deceitful, and beauty is vain; But a woman that feareth Jehovah, she shall be praised.
x.Darby: Gracefulness is deceitful and beauty is vain; a woman [that] feareth Jehovah, she shall be praised.
x.KJV: Favour is deceitful, and beauty is vain: but a woman that feareth the Lord, she shall be praised.
x.YLT: The grace is false, and the beauty is vain, A woman fearing Jehovah, she may boast herself.

nt: Here, **The charm** and **the beauty** refer to these qualities in general, not any specific **charm** or **beauty**. If it would be helpful, you could use more natural expressions in your language. Alternate translation: [Any charm … any beauty]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **charm**, **falsehood**, and **beauty**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. See how you translated **falsehood** in [6:17](../06/17.md) and **beauty** in [6:25](../06/25.md). Alternate translation: [What is charming is false and what is beautiful is vapor]

The parallelism between this half of the verse and the second half indicates that **charm** and **beauty** refer to the physical attractiveness of women. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [A woman’s charm can be deceptive and a woman’s beauty is vapor]
Here, Lemuel’s mother speaks of the disappearance of **beauty** as if it were a **vapor** that quickly goes away. See how you translated the same use of **vapor** in [21:6](../21/06.md).

Here, **a woman**, **she**, and **herself** refer to a type of **woman** in general, not a specific **woman**. If it would be helpful, you could use more natural expressions in your language. Alternate translation: [any woman fearful of Yahweh, that woman herself will be praised]
This half of the verse is a strong contrast with the previous half. Use the most natural way in your language to indicate a contrast. Alternate translation: [by contrast, a woman fearful of Yahweh]

If your language does not use this passive form, you could express the idea in active form or in another way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [people will certainly praise her]

The intensive pronoun **herself** represents the pronoun “her” that Lemuel’s mother uses in the original even though the verb translated as **she will be praised** already includes this meaning. Doing this adds emphasis to what she is saying. If your language uses explicit pronouns for emphasis, you may want to use that construction in your translation. If not, your language may have other ways of bringing out this emphasis. Alternate translation: [she will certainly be praised] or [people will certainly praise her]

x.ASV: Give her of the fruit of her hands; And let her works praise her in the gates.
x.Darby: Give her of the fruit of her hands, and let her own works praise her in the gates.
x.KJV: Give her of the fruit of her hands; and let her own works praise her in the gates.
x.YLT: Give ye to her of the fruit of her hands, And her works do praise her in the gates!

nt: In this verse, **her** refers to the “woman fearful of Yahweh” mentioned in the previous verse. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state this explicitly. Alternate translation: [to a woman fearful of Yahweh … that woman’s hands, and let that woman’s works praise her]

Here, **the fruit of her hands** could refer to: (1) any kind of reward that the woman deserves for her hard work. Alternate translation: [the reward for her work]; (2) the money that the woman has earned by selling the clothing she made in [31:13](../31/13.md), like the nearly identical phrase “from the fruit of her palms” in [31:16](../31/16.md). Alternate translation: [from the money she has earned]

Here, Lemuel’s mother speaks of people praising this woman because of **her works** as if the **works** were people who were the ones praising her. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and let people praise her for her works]
See how you translated the same use of **the gates** in [1:21](../01/21.md) and [31:23](../31/23.md).
